title: LCA of a Smartphone: Why Lifetime Matters Most
sub: A cradle-to-grave assessment of smartphone service per year of use, comparing one-, three- and five-year use, a refurbished phone and a repair-and-reuse scenario.
pdf: Case 08 — LCA of a Smartphone: Executive Summary
fu: Providing smartphone service to one user for one year in Germany
ref: Baseline: 1/3 of a 180 g smartphone (used three years), its charger share, packaging, three-year charging electricity divided per year, and end-of-life treatment
boundary: Cradle-to-grave: raw-material extraction, integrated circuits and components, display and battery, final assembly, packaging, global transport, consumer charging, repair, refurbishment, reuse, recycling and disposal
geo: Components and assembly in East Asia; use and end-of-life in Germany
method: EF 3.1 characterisation; IPCC AR6 GWP100; ADP (ultimate reserves) for minerals and metals
alloc: Refurbished scenario allocates 25% of original production burdens to the second user (lifetime-based); repair parts attributed to the life they extend; recycling via cut-off
cutoff: Flows <1% of mass and energy excluded (adhesives, small connectors) with cumulative exclusions <5%; network and data-centre energy excluded
dq: Manufacturer product environmental reports, peer-reviewed smartphone LCAs, ecoinvent electronics datasets. Overall data quality Medium; Low for integrated-circuit manufacturing
srcShort: Illustrative model; parameters within ranges from manufacturer product environmental reports, Fairphone LCAs, Clément et al. (2020) and ecoinvent electronics datasets.
loop: Circular loop: repair, refurbishment and resale; recovery of gold, copper, cobalt and other metals
exec:
This case study assesses smartphone service for one user for one year and compares five lifetime and circularity scenarios. Smartphones are high-volume products with concentrated environmental impacts in manufacturing, and they are now subject to EU ecodesign and energy-labelling rules (applying from June 2025) that require spare parts, battery durability and repair information.
In the baseline (a new phone used for three years), the illustrative result is 18.1 kg CO2e per year. Over 90% comes from production, with integrated circuits alone contributing nearly half. Charging contributes only about 7%.
Because production dominates, lifetime is the main lever. Replacing the phone every year triples the annual footprint (51.7 kg CO2e). Using it for five years with one battery replacement reduces it by 34% to 12.0 kg. A refurbished phone used by a second owner reaches 9.4 kg per year, and keeping a phone for six years with two repairs reaches 10.3 kg.
Recommendations focus on repairability, software support, refurbishment channels and take-back. For CSRD, results support ESRS E1 (Scope 3 Categories 1 and 11), E5 (critical raw materials, product lifetime, e-waste) and S2 (conflict minerals and supply-chain labour). Companies can also use the results to inform device policies for their own workforce.
overview:
A smartphone integrates dozens of components made from more than 50 elements, including gold, tantalum, tin, tungsten, cobalt and rare earths. The most impactful components are semiconductors, which require energy-intensive fabrication in cleanrooms.
The purpose of this LCA is to show how product lifetime and circular strategies change impacts, to support product design, corporate device procurement and policy discussions on repairability.
goal: The goal is to support device design, corporate IT procurement and circular-economy strategy by quantifying how the annual footprint of a smartphone changes with lifetime, repair and refurbishment. The audience is product teams, IT procurement, sustainability teams and policymakers.

stages.what: Mining and refining of metals and minerals: aluminium, copper, gold, tin, tantalum, tungsten, cobalt, lithium, rare earths.
stages.ew: ≈120 MJ and 360 L water per phone
stages.em: CO2, SO2, toxic emissions from mining

stages.what: Fabrication of processors, memory and other chips; printed circuit boards and passive components.
stages.in: Silicon wafers, ultra-pure water, electricity, process gases
stages.ew: ≈450 MJ and 660 L water per phone
stages.as: Taiwanese and Korean grids; advanced node logic

stages.what: OLED display and lithium-ion battery production.
stages.in: Glass, organic materials, cobalt, lithium, graphite, electricity

stages.so: Excessive overtime, student labour risks reported in the sector

stages.what: Production of the box, inserts and documentation.
stages.as: Plastic-free fibre packaging; no charger included

stages.what: Air freight to Europe and distribution to retail.
stages.em: CO2 including high-altitude effects not counted
stages.tr: 9,000 km by air; 500 km by truck
stages.as: Air freight typical for high-value electronics

stages.what: Daily charging over the phone's life.
stages.as: German grid; network and data-centre energy excluded

stages.what: Repair, refurbishment, collection and recycling, or storage in drawers and disposal.
stages.ew: Energy for recycling (smelting of circuit boards)
stages.so: Informal e-waste processing in export markets
stages.as: Only ≈20% enter formal recycling; many are stored unused

hot.why: Chip fabrication needs large amounts of electricity, ultra-pure water and fluorinated gases. It is about 48% of the climate result and the main water hotspot.
Because production dominates, replacing a phone after one year nearly triples the annual footprint compared with three years of use.
Gold, tantalum, tin, tungsten and cobalt dominate mineral resource use and carry human-rights and conflict-financing risks.
Most phones are stored unused or discarded; only about a fifth enter formal recycling, and many critical metals are not recovered.

sens.t: Sensitivity: years of use per phone
sens.yl: kg CO₂e per year of use
sens.note: Lifetime is varied without repairs; charging electricity is held at 4 kWh per year.
sens.interp: Extending life from three to five years cuts annual impact by about 37%. Doubling the grid intensity for charging changes results by only 1.2 kg per year, confirming that production dominates.

wf: Extend to 5 years with battery swap

ci.stage: Integrated circuits are the largest stage by far, followed by display and battery and raw materials. Use-phase charging is small.
ci.stage_e: Energy demand follows the same pattern: chip fabrication dominates.
ci.stage_w: Water consumption is driven by ultra-pure water in chip fabs and by mining.
ci.donut: Over 90% of the annual footprint is embodied in production, which is why lifetime is the key lever.
ci.sankey: Of each 180 g phone, only about 40 g reach formal recycling; 70 g sit unused in drawers, holding recoverable materials.
ci.heat: ICs are a hotspot for climate, energy, water and toxicity; raw materials for resources and toxicity.
ci.scen: Every scenario that keeps a device in use longer lowers impacts per year; refurbishment gives the lowest result.
ci.radar: The one-year scenario dominates every axis; refurbishment and repair scenarios are the smallest profiles.
ci.wf: Lifetime extension delivers more than half of the reduction; supply-chain renewable electricity is the second lever.

interp.m: For smartphones, the most effective climate action is to make and buy fewer devices by using them longer. Charging efficiency is a minor issue.
interp.a: Lifetime; IC fabrication energy and die area; allocation for refurbished phones; grid intensity in East Asia.
interp.u: IC data are the largest uncertainty (die area and node vary widely); repair and refurbishment burdens vary by service model.
interp.can: Lifetime extension, repair and refurbishment substantially reduce annual impacts.
interp.cannot: The study cannot rank smartphone brands or models, and does not include network and data-centre energy.
interp.d: Device-lifetime policies for corporate fleets, refurbished procurement, design for repair, spare-part and software-support commitments.

recs: Design for repair (replaceable batteries and screens, standard fasteners) and long software support; reduce IC die area where possible.
Set minimum device lifetimes in corporate IT policy; buy refurbished devices; require take-back services.
Use renewable electricity in fabs and assembly; increase recycled content (aluminium, tin, cobalt, rare earths).
Offer repair, trade-in and certified refurbished devices; communicate lifetime and repair options.
Increase collection of unused phones through incentives; recover more critical metals from circuit boards.
Track device lifetimes and refurbished share; report Scope 3 Cat. 1 for IT hardware; include conflict-mineral due diligence in S2 disclosures.
Enforce ecodesign repairability requirements; support right-to-repair and collection incentives.

take: For a smartphone, the greenest phone is the one you already have: keeping it for five years instead of three cuts its annual footprint by about a third, and buying refurbished cuts it by about half.
biz: Set longer device lifetimes, buy refurbished where possible and require repair and take-back services; for brands, design for repair and extend software support as core climate and circularity levers.
assume: Production ≈50 kg CO2e per phone; charging 4 kWh/year on the German grid; air freight; 25% production allocation to second user in refurbishment; network and data-centre energy excluded.
